item.title: Rate--burst safety languages: the Farey structure of the burst boundary and discrimination under erasures
item.description: arXiv:2611.28606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A leaky-bucket constraint with rate \(\rho\) and burst \(B\) allows at most \(\rho n+B\) costly steps in every window of \(n\) consecutive steps. The infinite 0/1 words that satisfy it form a safety language. For a finite graph with edge costs 0 and 1, we study the least burst at which the cost word of some infinite path lies in this language, as a function of the real rate. This function is the exact tolerance of a monitor that distinguishes two finite-state systems observed through an erasure channel with a leaky-bucket bound. The language is \(\omega\)-regular at every rational rate but not at irrational rates once the burst reaches 1, so ultimately periodic witnesses do not come from automata theory. We prove directly that simple lassos suffice at all real rates and that all breakpoints of the boundary lie in the Farey sequence of order N for a graph with N vertices. One lasso has a tight bound of order N to the power 2/3 on its affine pieces, whereas the choice among paths creates downward jumps and boundaries that are neither convex nor concave. One evaluation at the mediant of each Farey interval recovers the affine piece and an optimal lasso, and a greatest-fixed-point computation over decreasing integer bursts yields the whole function in polynomial time and linear working space. We also compute discrimination horizons and extend the Farey structure to turn-based safety games.
item.dc:creator: Lihui Dong, Zhuo Li

item.title: Spatial Ensemble Logic for Biomedical Imaging: Geometric Element Ensembles in Euclidean Space
item.description: arXiv:2611.29105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics over metric monoids whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We study its member over the Euclidian space, called Spatial Ensemble Logic (SEL), for biomedical images. Geometric element ensembles (GELs) represent atomic propositions by finite lists of effectively presented semi-algebraic sets, principally closed balls. Translation, dilation and erosion preserve individual balls up to emptiness in any dimension. Translation and dilation act element-wise, but element-wise erosion gives only an inner bound. For $k\geq 2$, finite unions of balls are closed under neither intersection nor erosion. We therefore separate record representation from the evaluation domain. Our main result is a satisfaction-preserving translation over GELs into the first-order theory of real closed fields. It yields computable semi-algebraic satisfaction sets, decidable model checking and finite real algebraic evidence. For a fixed formula and dimension, model checking has polynomial data complexity under stated rationality and bounded-degree assumptions. Combined complexity is PSPACE-hard and in EXPSPACE. On the line, rational interval data admit linear-arithmetic evaluation with rational evidence, under rationality assumptions on the norm, query and evaluation point. For $k\geq 2$, rational balls can force irrational witnesses. Lower and upper annotation bounds propagate through formulas. Synthesis of a ball ensemble is decidable within a prescribed budget of balls and undecidable without one. In a vascular use case, medial ball ensembles decide calibre and stenosis queries at stored centers by comparing stored numbers. We also examine how far evaluation can proceed element-wise when the union forming a support is deferred to the point of evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Guo-Qiang Zhang

item.title: $\mathsf{Y} \& \mathsf{X}$: Intermediate Logics of Convex Hulls and Cross-Polytopes
item.description: arXiv:2611.29298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate two logics of geometric Kripke frames: $\mathsf{Y}$, defined by finite convex hulls, and $\mathsf{X}$, defined by cross-polytopes. We characterize the validity of the Kreisel--Putnam axiom on convex hull frames by means of convex independence. Our main technical results concern several reductions obtained using two translations, $C$ and $D$. In particular, we show that $\mathsf{X}$ is invariant under $C$, while $\mathsf{Y}$ is invariant under $D$. Moreover, the same translation $D$ reduces Medvedev logic to every logic in the interval $[\mathsf{Y}',\mathsf{Med}]$, where $\mathsf{Y}'$ is a naturally defined intermediate logic strictly between $\mathsf{Y}$ and $\mathsf{Med}$. Together with geometric arguments, these reductions establish that $\mathsf{Y}$, $\mathsf{X}$, and $\mathsf{Cheq}$ are pairwise incomparable, while each lies strictly between $\mathsf{PL}$ and Medvedev logic. We also prove that every logic in $[\mathsf{Y},\mathsf{Med}]$ is not finitely axiomatizable and that this interval contains continuum many distinct logics. In addition, every logic in $[\mathsf{Y}',\mathsf{Med}]$ is undecidable. We prove that $\mathsf{X}$ is undecidable and $\mathsf{Y}\in \Pi^0_1$. In particular, we show that it is decidable whether a finite poset is isomorphic to a finite convex hull frame, and that the logics determined by configurations of a bounded number of points are decidable. Finally, we extend our study to infinite convex hull frames. We show that inclusion yields $\mathsf{KC}$, whereas reverse inclusion yields $\mathsf{IPC}$. For the latter result, we use the Cantor set to construct $p$-morphisms onto arbitrary finite rooted frames.
item.dc:creator: Yumin Ji, Han Xiao

item.title: Two Primes Suffice for Definable Graph Canonisation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study inflationary fixed-point logic on finite simple graphs with unordered vertices and an ordered number sort. For a prime $r$, the quantifier $M_r$ tests whether the number of relations satisfying a formula is nonzero modulo $r$. For any distinct primes $p$ and $q$, the logic with $M_p$ and $M_q$ defines the adjacency matrix of a canonical copy on the number sort. On labelled inputs this matrix is computable in deterministic polynomial time with an oracle that tests whether the number of satisfying assignments of a Boolean circuit is nonzero modulo $p$. For each prime $p$, the logic with $M_p$ alone cannot define a canonical copy on all graphs. The primes also differ on Boolean queries. There is a single first-order formula $\beta(S)$ on vertex sets such that $M_q S \beta(S)$ is undefinable with $M_p$ alone whenever $p \ne q$. For a positive integer-valued function $g$, consider the class of all graphs $G$ with at most $g(|V(G)|)$ automorphisms. For each fixed prime $p$, the logic with $M_p$ canonises this class exactly when $g$ is bounded.
item.dc:creator: Vaani Goenka, Aalok Thakkar

item.title: Probabilistic Timed Automata with Multiple Sure and Threshold Objectives
item.description: arXiv:2611.29365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Probabilistic timed automata extend the classical timed automata formalism with discrete probabilistic choice over edges. We consider the case of the verification of a combination of multiple objectives of probabilistic timed automata, where the objectives can be non-probabilistic (referring to sure satisfaction of all behaviors) and probabilistic (referring to a probability threshold), and refer to reachability or $\omega$-regular properties on executions expressed using parity conditions. We show that existing algorithms for multiple objectives for finite-state Markov decision processes can be applied, using the classical region-graph construction, to obtain algorithms for the corresponding objectives of probabilistic timed automata. In particular, the verification of a probabilistic timed automata against multiple probabilistic-threshold sink-reachability objectives subject to the almost-sure divergence of time is EXPTIME-complete, while verification against the combination of a sure property, including sure divergence of time, and a single probabilistic-threshold parity objective is in NEXPTIME $\cap$ coNEXPTIME.
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Sproston

item.title: Hashing Theorems Modulo Rewrites and Binder Permutation Enables Equivalence Search over 200k Mathlib Theorems
item.description: arXiv:2611.29603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Like all code, Lean libraries accumulate technical debt and structural deficiencies over the course of their development. A particular concern is duplicate theorems: different parts of a big library can unwittingly contain and prove the same theorem, duplicating maintenance efforts. Tools can help detect redundancy and clean up. For instance, Mathlib's duplicate-declarations linter compares theorem types syntactically after sorting top-level binders and erasing binder information and universe levels. If detecting an equivalence requires unfolding, reorientation, or logical transformations, it escapes this comparison. In this work, we present a method to detect theorems which are equivalent with regard to argument order and currying/uncurrying of dependent types. We implement our method for Lean. By applying it to Mathlib, a library of more than 200k theorems, we demonstrate that it is computationally cheap and scalable. We discuss how our work may enhance efforts to tackle the maintenance burden of Lean libraries.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Le{\ss}mann, Simon Henniger, Gabriel Poesia, Nada Amin

item.title: TPTL-dist: A Formalised Calculus with Proof Automation for Verifying Real-Time Distributed Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.29738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce TPTL-dist, a temporal logic and labelled sequent calculus for specifying and verifying real-time distributed systems. TPTL-dist is formalised in Agda to provide machine-checked correctness and tool support, including automation through a proof search that runs inside Agda. The logic extends Timed Propositional Temporal Logic (TPTL) with past operators, freeze quantification, comparisons between time expressions, domain-specific atoms, and an induction principle on time. We provide a world-based semantics, develop an interval-annotated calculus, and establish its soundness w.r.t. the semantics. To demonstrate its expressiveness, we encode standard distributed system patterns, and we carry out a mechanised proof of a key real-time property of the Pistis Byzantine broadcast protocol. Our results show that TPTL-dist provides a uniform, mechanised framework for reasoning about temporal properties of distributed systems.
item.dc:creator: Javier Enr\'iquez Mendoza, Sam Speight, Vincent Rahli

item.title: Higher Duality Theory: Geometric HoTT and Classifying $\infty$-Toposes
item.description: arXiv:2611.29830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop geometric homotopy type theory (geometric HoTT), which gives a dependent language for constructions preserved by inverse images of geometric morphisms. We give a homotopy-coherent calculus for geometric HoTT and extend the classical duality between geometric logic and classifying toposes to Grothendieck $\infty$-toposes. For each geometric type theory, the $\infty$-category of contexts generated by its rules is equivalent to its classifying $\infty$-topos. As the theory varies, the classifier gives a duality of $(\infty,2)$-categories between geometric HoTT theories with interpretations and Grothendieck $\infty$-toposes with geometric morphisms. We then construct a universal family of classifying $\infty$-toposes whose fiber at each presentation of a theory is the classifying $\infty$-topos of that theory. We also construct a universal family of classifying $\infty$-toposes with coherent transport along Morita equivalences of theories. Geometric HoTT thus serves as an internal language for Grothendieck $\infty$-toposes, extending the role of geometric logic in classical topos theory to the realm of $\infty$-topos theory.
item.dc:creator: Yoshihiro Maruyama

item.title: Higher Realizability Toposes
item.description: arXiv:2611.29832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building on $\infty$-tripos theory, we develop a theory of realizability $\infty$-toposes. We apply $\infty$-tripos theory to construct the function, modified, and Krivine realizability $\infty$-toposes. We recover the Lawvere-Tierney nucleus $j$ that specifies local truth in each construction by exhibiting, for any $n\geq1$, a single family of Eilenberg-MacLane $n$-types whose fibre at an ambient truth value $p$ is contractible after sheafification precisely when $j(p)$ holds. In function realizability, we relate identity types to descriptive set theory. For each $n\geq 2$, we construct a univalent classifier $U_n$ of exact truncation height $n+1$. As maps from Baire space into $U_n$ vary, the sets of inputs admitting a global path from the assigned code to the terminal code are exactly the $G_\delta$ subsets of Baire space. After exponentiation by Baire space, the analogous test against the constant map at the terminal code yields exactly the coanalytic sets, at the same truncation height. In modified realizability, a closed proof of local existence under a stable numerical precondition yields a total recursive function together with a coherent proof that its output satisfies the specification whenever the precondition holds. In Krivine realizability, contextual choice for $(n-1)$-truncated families over suitable $n$-types recovers the subterminal defining the Boolean localization. Binary cohomology distinguishes slices of Anel-Awodey-Barton's effective $\infty$-topos even when they share the same ordinary Hyland effective topos and their bases have equivalent spaces of global points. Hyland's effective topos thus occurs as the category of zero-types in infinitely many pairwise inequivalent realizability $\infty$-toposes (recovering Hyland's effective topos as the category of zero-types does not uniquely determine an effective $\infty$-topos).
item.dc:creator: Yoshihiro Maruyama

item.title: Tableau Consequence under Positive Contexts: A Reconstruction of Walukiewicz's Completeness Proof
item.description: arXiv:2611.30009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a positive-context lifting theorem for tableau consequence in the modal $\mu$-calculus: under explicit syntactic hypotheses, $\mathcal T_B\Rightarrow\mathcal T_C$ induces $\mathcal T_{A(B)}\Rightarrow\mathcal T_{A(C)}$. The proof orders instances of the given relation by birth time and assigns overlapping formula occurrences to the oldest supporting instance. A corollary gives bidirectional replacement by automaton normal form inside positive contexts. Together with a separate unfolding consequence lemma and ANF bisimulation, the lifting theorem yields a self-contained reconstruction of Walukiewicz's completeness proof for Kozen's axiomatisation and makes its least-fixpoint step more transparent. We also give a finite parity-game proof of regular-refutation existence and a two-sided transfer from tableau consequence to thin refutations.
item.dc:creator: Kuniaki Tamura

item.title: Sheaf Semantics of Probabilistic Programs
item.description: arXiv:2611.30692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finding denotational models of probabilistic languages that support sampling from continuous distributions is difficult: the existence of continuous distributions means that measure-theoretic objects are needed to define the semantics. A challenging task on top of this is logical reasoning with respect to the semantic model: in the case of probabilistic programs, the desired properties to reason about include the distributions, expected value and the probabilistic (in)dependence of outputs. This paper introduces a monadic semantics for higher-order probabilistic programs with continuous distributions based on Simpson's theory of probability sheaves and the internal logic of atomic sheaves. We prove that our semantics forms a model of the $\nu$-calculus. Furthermore, using the well-behavedness of the semantic domain and the internal logic of the topos, we derive the first higher-order probabilistic Hoare logic with rigorous treatment of continuous random variables, higher-order functions, and independence.
item.dc:creator: Shing Hin Ho, Nicolas Wu, Azalea Raad

item.title: Lean Census: A Distributional Analysis of AI-Generated Lean Code
item.description: arXiv:2611.28430v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We compare two human-written and four AI-generated Lean libraries with Mathlib through the distributions of simple statistics of their code. For each library we measure inline claims in proofs, proof length, how often each declaration is used, and design choices such as instances and private declarations, and we read each against the variation among Mathlib's own areas. The AI-generated libraries have more inline claims per theorem, longer proofs, fewer instances, and more private declarations than the human-written ones. We release the code for the analysis as a package, lean-census, at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census.
item.dc:creator: Justin Asher, Pietro Pellegrino

item.title: Bound to be Complete: Efficient Verification for SQL Equivalence via U-Expressions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated verification of SQL query equivalence is a fundamental problem in database area. Recent works developed verifiers with guaranteed completeness, which can generate counterexamples to disprove non-equivalent queries and are useful in various scenarios. However, they have to solve complex formulas and can fail to produce counterexamples within a reasonable time budget. This paper presents a new complete verifier called SQLution, which not only greatly reduces the verification time, but also supports more SQL features. The key insight is to represent SQL semantics using U-expression, a functional algebra that can model SQL with significantly simpler formulas than prior works, thereby leading to more efficient SMT solving. To turn this insight into a practical verifier, SQLution further tackles two technical challenges associated with modeling SQL using U-expression, namely, the lack of tuple ordering and the presence of unbounded summations. In particular, to support tuple ordering, SQLution proposes order semantics encoding which combines U-expressions with first-order logic. To handle unbounded summation, SQLution introduces unbounded summation expansion to transform them into bounded summations, which can be directly encoded into FOL formulas. Evaluation shows that compared with state-of-the-art verifiers, SQLution can support all 271 non-equivalent query pairs derived from the Spider dataset and reduces verification time by up to 98.6%.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Ding, Zhaoguo Wang, Zuming Jiang, Haibo Chen, Jinyang Li, Ruzica Piskac

item.title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers
item.description: arXiv:2611.28704v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.
item.dc:creator: Tobias Philipp

item.title: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28727v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget $k$ (with both end labels fixed when $k$ is odd), the smallest size on which $d$ mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: $d+1$ while $d\le k$, then $2d-k+1$, and beyond $d=\lceil 3k/2\rceil+k-1$ doubling the size adds exactly $k$ mistakes. Unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points correspond to $k=2j$ and size $m+1$, and a single interval gives the thresholds $1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,\dots$. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below $10^5$. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with $O(\log m)$ time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within $0.64$ of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for $m\le70$). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Miit Daga, Swarna Priya Ramu

item.title: Taming Fitch's and Humberstone's Paradoxes
item.description: arXiv:2611.29149v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fitch's Paradox says that if every true proposition is knowable, then every true proposition is known. Humberstone's Paradox states that if every true proposition is known by at least one of a set of finitely many agents, then some agent in that set knows every true proposition. Both paradoxes give rise to surprising and unacceptable consequences. In this paper, we diagnose a crucial tacit presupposition underlying these paradoxes, namely that the domain of propositions is closed under Boolean operations such as intersection and union, and offer a uniform resolution. We argue that the paradoxical inferences rely implicitly on this closure assumption. By adopting weak propositionally quantified modal logics that drop these closure conditions, we provide a semantically motivated account that blocks both paradoxes. The restriction on universal instantiation is not an ad hoc technical device, but reflects a conception of propositions as graspable objects of epistemic attitudes, on which the domain of propositions need not be closed under Boolean operations, since some Boolean combinations of graspable propositions may not themselves be graspable.
item.dc:creator: Jie Fan

item.title: A logic of strong contingency
item.description: arXiv:2611.29182v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, inspired by the notions of contingency and strong possibility, we propose a notion which may be called 'strong contingency'. This notion can be seen as a mixture of contingency and strong possibility. We investigate the logic with strong contingency as a sole primitive modality, including its bisimulation notion, expressivity, frame definability, and axiomatizations. It turns out that this logic is expressively incomparable with the standard modal logic and the logic of contingency even over the class of S5-models, and less expressive than the logic of strong possibility and weak necessity over the class of S5-models. Besides, as the introduction of the inequality into the semantics makes the completeness proof much harder, instead of showing the completeness via a canonical model construction, we reduce the soundness and strong completeness of the involved proof systems to those of the existing proof systems in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Jie Fan

item.title: A detailed verification of Neary's PCP(5) construction
item.description: arXiv:2611.29559v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neary proved that the Post correspondence problem remains undecidable for instances with five pairs of words. We give a detailed verification of his construction. We first verify the undecidability of the restricted binary tag-system halting problem used in the reduction. We then prove both directions of the reduction to the five-pair problem, using the longer closing pair proposed by Rote. In particular, we show that every solution of the constructed PCP instance yields a halting computation of the simulated tag system.
item.dc:creator: Vesa Halava

item.title: Deterministic Proper Positive-Only Learning Is Independent of ZFC
item.description: arXiv:2611.29737v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Binary classification from positive-only samples is a variant of PAC learning in which the learner receives i.i.d. samples only from the positive region of an unknown target concept, but is evaluated on the full distribution. Improper learnability in this model has a textbook characterization, whereas proper learnability has remained open for decades. Recent work characterized it for learners with access to randomness, and showed that, unlike in PAC learning, some classes are properly learnable with randomness but not without it, leaving the deterministic case open. We show that this case cannot be resolved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC): there is a class of VC dimension two whose deterministic proper learnability is independent of ZFC, even though a randomized learner provably learns it. Moreover, no dimension of finite character, a desirable property shared by most dimensions in learning theory, characterizes deterministic proper learnability. We also show that the size of the domain is decisive. In ZFC, deterministic proper learnability has a combinatorial characterization on every domain whose cardinality is below a certain threshold, including every countable domain. In contrast, this characterization fails on every domain of sufficiently large cardinality. Under the generalized continuum hypothesis, this threshold is sharp: it is the exact cardinality at which the characterization starts to fail. Finally, our proofs introduce new tools, based on the Erdos--Rado partition theorem, that may be of broader interest.
item.dc:creator: Shai Ben-David, Farnam Mansouri, Anay Mehrotra

item.title: Categorical Foundations of AI Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.29998v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We follow the idea of separating intelligence from execution and give the categorical foundations of AI agents: the transformers, the agents, and the orchestrations and choreographies of AI agents are categorized, and which also include their coalgebras and algebras.
item.dc:creator: Yong Wang

item.title: Complexity of the Infinity and the Modulo-Counting Quantifiers in Automatic Structures
item.description: arXiv:2611.30944v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automatic structures allow us to decide their first-order theory using automata-theoretic techniques. The complexity of this decision problem for formulas in prenex normal form depends on the quantifier alternation depth, e.g., it is PSPACE-complete for formulas with quantifier-prefix $\exists\exists\cdots\exists$. Blumensath observed that the decidability also holds if one extends first-order logic with the infinity quantifier. His decision procedure introduces many more quantifier alternations such that, even for formulas with quantifier prefix $\exists^\infty\exists^\infty\cdots\exists^\infty$ of length $n$, his decision procedure runs in $(2n-1)$-fold exponential space. We show that this is not necessary. To be more precise, we prove that handling the infinity quantifier is not more costly than handling the existential quantifier. On the other hand, we also show that addition of the modulo-counting quantifier to first-order logic results in a much higher complexity.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Klimmer, Dietrich Kuske, Sebastian Pfau

item.title: Complexity as Axiomatic Incompleteness
item.description: arXiv:2408.10211v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: IInformation theory has long sought to uncover the universal laws governing complex systems. Yet information is not merely quantified; it is also interpreted by observers.We formalize this cognitive aspect through a Generalized Incompleteness Theory (GIC), which integrates axiomatic logic, Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, and G\"odel's incompleteness theorem to establish a connection between complexity and formal incompleteness. We introduce the notions of interpreter-based information and PAC complexity, demonstrating that certain outputs can be PAC-learnable even when their corresponding interpreters cannot be constructed. We further show that every nontrivial formal system contains a PAC-learnable incompleteness space of dimension \(2^n-n-1\). The GIC framework unifies several foundational results-including Cantor's diagonal argument, G\"odel's incompleteness theorem, and the Turing halting problem-within a categorical and topological framework. We further show that physical models, including four-dimensional spacetime in relativity and the 11- and 26-dimensional spaces arising in string theory, admit natural correspondences with incompleteness spaces, while critical states can be understood in terms of symmetry-breaking selections of axioms. Our framework identifies incompleteness as a universal feature underlying complexity, criticality, and observability, thereby revealing fundamental limits on description and cognition in any axiomatizable theory.
item.dc:creator: Zhifeng Ma, Zhangang Han

item.title: Ensemble Logic
item.description: arXiv:2408.14443v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We interpret formulas over metric monoids, that is, commutative monoids equipped with translation-invariant metrics. Displacement evaluates a formula at a translated point, while bounded existence and bounded universality evaluate it at some or every point of a window of prescribed length. Quantification over points and lengths allows the same variable to occur in the parameters of several operators. This provides a common framework for temporal and spatial reasoning in discrete, dense and multi-dimensional settings. Our main result establishes a sharp undecidability boundary for satisfiability over the natural numbers: satisfiability is undecidable already for formulas $\exists N\,\exists n\,\Psi$ in which $\Psi$ is built from the letters of a fixed alphabet by conjunction, disjunction, displacement and bounded universality. We prove this by a reduction from Post's Correspondence Problem. We also present results, in part from companion work, that place this theorem in the general theory of EL. These include an atomic-displacement normal form for covariant windows and composition laws for discrete and dense time. The discrete logic admits an embedding of linear temporal logic, defines the accepting runs of every B\"uchi automaton, and has a sound equational calculus. For the rational logic, we show that every fixed formula can be evaluated in polynomial time on interval models in which atomic propositions are interpreted by finite unions of intervals. Finally, we represent timed words over positions and real time and compare two window geometries; with rectangular windows, two shared lengths yield undecidability on finite timed words.
item.dc:creator: Guo-Qiang Zhang

item.title: Symmetries of Dependency Quantified Boolean Formulas
item.description: arXiv:2410.15848v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Symmetry breaking is a standard technique for reducing redundancy in automated reasoning, with well-developed theories for SAT and QBF. In this paper we study symmetries of dependency quantified Boolean formulas (DQBF), a generalisation of QBF which allows for explicit quantifier dependencies. The possibility of incomparable dependency sets makes extending existing QBF techniques non-trivial. We develop a theoretical framework for syntactic and semantic symmetries of DQBF that accounts for these dependency constraints. Building on this framework we establish a general lex-leader symmetry-breaking construction that strictly generalises the corresponding construction for QBF, using a lex-permissibility condition to ensure that local transformations respect the dependencies. We complement this construction with a canonisation method that exploits problem-specific symmetries without requiring lex-permissibility. Proof-of-concept experiments demonstrate the benefits of lex-leader symmetry breaking and the substantial additional gains provided by canonisation predicates for the succinct pigeonhole principle, although the impact of symmetry breaking is solver-dependent.
item.dc:creator: Paul Seip, Clemens Hofstadler, Manuel Kauers, Martina Seidl

item.title: Undecidability of the Emptiness Problem of Deterministic Propositional While Programs with Graph Loop: Hypothesis Elimination Using Loops
item.description: arXiv:2504.20415v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that the emptiness (unsatisfiability) problem is undecidable and $\mathrm{\Pi}^{0}_{1}$-complete for deterministic propositional while programs with (graph) loop. To this end, we introduce a hypothesis elimination procedure in propositional while programs using loops. Using this, we give reductions from the complement of the periodic domino problem, where the numbers of actions and primitive tests can be reduced by two and one, respectively. Moreover, as a corollary via hypothesis eliminations, we also show that the equational theory is $\mathrm{\Pi}^{0}_{1}$-complete for the positive calculus of relations with transitive closure and difference. Additionally, we show that the emptiness problem (on the class of all relational models) is \textsc{PSpace}-complete for the existential calculus of relations with transitive closure.
item.dc:creator: Yoshiki Nakamura

item.title: G\"odel-Tarski Translation for Constructive Logics with Transitive Closure
item.description: arXiv:2603.05131v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce the semantically-defined constructive propositional dynamic logics of regular programs $\sf CPDL$ and $\sf WPDL$, respectively extending the basic constructive modal logic $\sf CK$ and its Wijesekera-style variant $\sf WK$. Using translations between our logics and $\sf PDL$, we show that both $\sf CPDL$ and $\sf WPDL$ are {\sc ExpTime}-complete and enjoy an exponential-size finite model property. In particular, their diamond-free fragment, restricted to a single atomic program and its reflexive transitive closure is already {\sc ExpTime}-complete, thereby settling the conjecture of Afshari et al. By embedding $\sf CS4$ and $\sf WS4$ into our logics, we show their validity problems are also in {\sc ExpTime}, improving the previously known {\sc NExpTime} upper bound obtained via finite model arguments.
item.dc:creator: Sof\'ia Santiago-Fern\'andez, David Fern\'andez-Duque, Joost J. Joosten

item.title: Coalgebraic Path Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2603.12204v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Axiomatizing covarieties of coalgebras for an endofunctor is less intuitive than axiomatizing varieties of algebras via equations (Dahlqvist and Schmid, 2022). Existing techniques come from coalgebraic modal logic, pattern avoidance specifications, and hidden algebra. We introduce equational path constraints, a well-behaved and relatively easy to describe class of finitary behavioural properties that provide an algebra-flavoured alternative to coequations. The basic idea is to assign a pair of values to each path through a coalgebra and posit that the two values coincide. We show that equational path constraints define covarieties and construct final coalgebras relative to equational path constraints in some concrete cases. We connect equational path constraints to coequations when values computed from paths live in a monad, and we compute an upper bound on the number of colours needed to express the coequation. One of our constructions is reminiscent of the initial/terminal sequences of (Ad\'amek, 1974) and (Barr, 1993). Motivating examples include commutativity conditions in automata theory, differential equations, bi-infinite streams, and frame conditions.
item.dc:creator: Todd Schmid

item.title: Extending CDCL to disjunctions of parity equations
item.description: arXiv:2605.15002v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Problems provably hard for Resolution are also provably hard for CDCL, but shorter proofs can sometimes be found using stronger proof systems such as Res($\oplus$), a generalization of Resolution to XNF formulas, whose constraints are disjunctions of parity equations, called linear clauses. While some solvers like CryptoMiniSat reason on Boolean clauses with separate parity equations in a system called CNF-XOR, general XNF reasoning is less explored. We present CDCL($\oplus$), a generalization of CDCL to XNF formulas that includes branching on arbitrary parity equations, linear-algebraic reasoning during unit propagation, and learning linear clauses in conflict analysis. Our key tool is the affine resolution rule, which generalizes classical resolution and allows translations of 1-UIP clause learning and variable elimination. We develop a theory of UIPs to show that we learn an asserting clause with the largest possible backjump, the same guarantee as classical CDCL. We prove that CDCL($\oplus$) not only produces Res($\oplus$) proofs, but also polynomially simulates Res($\oplus$) given nondeterministic decisions and restarts, much like the relationship between CDCL and Resolution. We implement CDCL($\oplus$) in our solver Xorcle, which cleanly adapts over a dozen major classical CDCL heuristics. We introduce the CSIDS decision heuristic, which selects decisions from activity-ranked clauses, and the LRUP($\oplus$) proof logging format. On a suite of cryptographic benchmarks, Xorcle is generally competitive with or outperforms Kissat, CaDiCaL, and CryptoMiniSat, and beats the concurrently developed XNF solver Xorricane. Additionally, Xorcle's reasoning and search alone (i.e., without detecting XORs) solves CNF versions of Tseitin formulas, perfect matching formulas, and bijective pigeonhole formulas with $n+1$ pigeons into $n$ holes using apparently polynomial running time.
item.dc:creator: Paul Beame, Glenn Sun

item.title: Containment of Conjunctive Queries with Negative Information over Semirings
item.description: arXiv:2610.27957v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the containment problem for (unions of) conjunctive queries ((U)CQs) with negative information on semiring-annotated databases. Our approach to negative information follows the treatment of negation proposed by Gr\"adel and Tannen (2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024) for first-order logic and fixed point logic which applies productively to large classes of semirings, including bounded distributive lattices, as well as the important provenance semirings studied for positive CQ containment by Green (2009). Negation features in (U)CQs along two dimensions: negated equalities (disequations), and negated relational atoms. We study complexity for each of them separately, as well as jointly. For disequations, we extend a methodology that proves the same complexity bounds as the ones already known for the standard Boolean semiring (in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) for most semirings of interest. Two prominent exceptions are $\mathbb{N}[X]$ and Trio(X) where the complexity bound for containment is in the second level of the counting hierarchy. For CQs with negated relational atoms we show that the complexity, surprisingly, is the same as that of the containment of CQs without negation when one considers model-defining and provenance-tracking interpretations (namely, nondeterministic polynomial time). Interestingly, among bounded distributive lattices, the Boolean two-element case is the only one where the complexity of the problem continues to be hard for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy for model-defining interpretations. Furthermore, we show that the complexity increases again for distributive lattices if we focus on other classes of interpretations. Finally, we consider queries that have both negated equalities and negated relational atoms and show that the complexity of containment continues to be that of the case with just negated equalities.
item.dc:creator: Guillermo Badia, Carles Noguera, Gaia Petreni, Alice Portone, Val Tannen

item.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
item.description: arXiv:2611.15108v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Proof-assistant kernels with strict propositions---Lean 4, Agda's Prop, and Coq/Rocq's SProp---build proof irrelevance into conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$), equating all derivations of a theorem. While natural for pure mathematics, judgmental proof irrelevance breaks provenance in verified scientific stores, where predicates, refinements, and institutional maps must distinguish independent derivations for consilience and counterfactual retraction; with subsingleton elimination, it also breaks normalization and algorithmic transitivity. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a kernel for provenance-preserving scientific stores. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes (Prop, Set, $\mathsf{Type}_k$ for $k \ge 1$), impredicative Prop, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types: conversion $\equiv$ is untyped orthogonal-CRS joinability, while proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($\mathsf{irrel} : \Pi P:\mathsf{Prop}.\,\Pi p,q:P.\,\mathsf{Id}\,P\,p\,q$). Second, coercion-free subsumption unifies cumulativity, $\Pi$-covariant subtyping, and ontology inclusions; its bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, match declarative typing, and compile to heuristic-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$) sound and complete relative to strong normalization. Third, we link external verifiers via constructive institutions (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize justification logic with Why-provenance $\mathsf{supp}(j,P)$, and type open-world knowledge graphs via TTR. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry.
item.dc:creator: Hans-Martin Will

item.title: Coalgebra for True Concurrency
item.description: arXiv:2611.19736v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give the coalgebra for true concurrency along the way paved by traditional coalgebra based on bisimulation. This coalgebra is based on truly concurrent bisimulation, and we give its definition and a simple truly concurrent process algebra.
item.dc:creator: Yong Wang

item.title: Taint Analysis via Heap-Aware Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2611.20453v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Taint analysis for C depends on how precisely the analysis tracks tainted values as they flow through memory objects. Without field sensitivity, a tainted object field can spuriously taint an entire object, producing significant false alarms. In this paper, we present a field-sensitive taint analysis that combines Data Structure Analysis (DSA) for field-sensitive points-to information with a data-flow analysis for tracking explicit dependencies. We identify that existing DSA-style analyses lose precision on a common object pattern: a C struct object that mixes scalar fields with a flexible array member. When such an array is accessed with symbolic indices, DSA loses points-to field sensitivity for the entire object, inflating false alarms in the data-flow analysis. To address this, we propose I-DSA, which extends DSA by representing field positions as intervals, so that a pointer with symbolic bounds merges only the fields within those bounds. We further develop a sound data-flow analysis based on abstract interpretation. We implement I-DSA on top of SeaDSA and the data-flow analysis inside Crab. Our tool targets LLVM IR and supports configurable taint policies by instrumenting the IR with taint intrinsics. Our experiments show that I-DSA reduces the false alarms caused by this pattern at little cost in the pointer analysis, that SVF, an inclusion-based pointer analysis, shows a similar field-sensitivity loss, and that our taint analysis scales better than PhASAR on real-world programs.
item.dc:creator: Yusen Su, Jorge A. Navas, Arie Gurfinkel

item.title: Hereditary permutations for simple types revisited: A baby case for University Algebra
item.description: arXiv:2611.26507v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is a classical result that the definable isomorphisms of the simply typed $\lambda$-calculus with function types are exactly the hereditary permutations, and that they are generated by $A \to B \to C \cong B \to A \to C$ and congruence. We give a new proof of this result that stays inside $\beta$-normal $\eta$-long typed terms and uses no completeness theorem: an induction that descends through both components of an isomorphism at once. It proceeds by showing that both components are linear terms: relevance follows from one of the inverse equations, and no copying from relevance of the other component. We then go one level up and prove a coherence theorem: two derivations of an isomorphism denote the same isomorphism if and only if they are equal modulo an explicit list of equations (groupoid laws, functoriality, involution, naturality and the braid equation), so these equations present the groupoid of isomorphisms, a hereditary version of the Coxeter presentation of the symmetric groups. All results are formalised in Agda, on intrinsically typed syntax with hereditary substitution, without postulates. The work is a case study for the syntactic completeness conjecture of University Algebra, a proposed solution of Tarski's high school algebra problem using dependent types, whose semantic counterpart is open. We explain the motivation and which parts of the method we expect to carry over.
item.dc:creator: Thorsten Altenkirch

item.title: Double negation stable h-propositions in cubical sets
item.description: arXiv:2209.15035v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give a construction of classifiers for double negation stable h-propositions in a variety of cubical set models of homotopy type theory and cubical type theory. This is used to give some relative consistency results: classifiers for double negation stable propositions exist in cubical sets whenever they exist in the metatheory; the Dedekind real numbers can be added to homotopy type theory without changing the consistency strength; we construct a model of homotopy type theory with extended Church's thesis, which states that all partial functions with double negation stable domain are computable.
item.dc:creator: Andrew W. Swan

item.title: JustLogic: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Deductive Reasoning in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2501.14851v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Logical reasoning is a critical component of Large Language Models (LLMs), and substantial research efforts in recent years have aimed to enhance their deductive reasoning abilities. However, existing deductive reasoning benchmarks suffer from significant constraints that restrict their utility, i.e., the lack of task complexity, the presence of prior knowledge as a confounder, and superficial error analysis. To address these deficiencies, we introduce JustLogic, a synthetically generated benchmark for evaluating deduction in propositional logic. Within this fragment, JustLogic is (i) complex, capable of generating a diverse range of linguistic patterns, vocabulary, and argument structures, (ii) prior knowledge independent, substantially reducing the advantage of models possessing prior knowledge so that questions are answerable from the given premises alone, and (iii) capable of in-depth error analysis on the heterogeneous effects of proof size and argument form on model accuracy. Our experimental results on JustLogic reveal that (i) several state-of-the-art (SOTA) reasoning LLMs score above the human average on JustLogic, although only DeepSeek R1's margin is significant on the matched items after correction for multiple comparisons, and (ii) the evaluated non-reasoning models score below the human average. Given the small human study (18 participants, seven questions each), these comparisons are indicative. All code and data are available at https://github.com/michaelchen-lab/JustLogic
item.dc:creator: Michael K. Chen, Xikun Zhang, Yao Li, Dacheng Tao

item.title: Attractors Is All You Need: Parity Games In Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2511.03752v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper provides a polynomial-time algorithm for solving parity games that runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot(n + m))$ time-ending a search that has taken decades. Unlike previous attractor-based algorithms, the presented algorithm only removes regions with a determined winner. The paper introduces a new type of attractor that can guarantee finding the minimal dominion of a parity game. The attractor runs in polynomial time and can peel the graph empty.
item.dc:creator: Rick van der Heijden

item.title: The Solver's Paradox for SAT
item.description: arXiv:2511.14665v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show in Rocq that every circuit verifier $v$ determines a formula $\psi_v$ whose satisfiability is $v$'s acceptance of its own diagonal claim: a satisfiability predicate thus behaves like a provability predicate. Every solver represented in the language misclassifies its own diagonal instance, and every verifier misjudges its own diagonal claim. We distinguish our result from (i) the refuters of Chen et al. (2024), which produce from the description of a solver an instance it gets wrong, and (ii) the refuter of Gutfreund et al. (2007) for efficient SAT solvers, which needs a hardness hypothesis and a simulation. Here the refuter is purely syntactic, and it separates evaluation of the language from its own expressions, not SAT from a resource-bounded class. The identity behind the fixed point uses no property of quotation; its reading as self-reference depends on the coding, and an injective recoding flips the branch. A truth table decides $\psi_v$ only from outside the language. Written inside, it is brute force: it settles the claim from above and has a diagonal instance of its own. This yields an unconditional certification hierarchy with tower growth, a quadratic lower bound on every internal evaluator, and an exponential lower bound on brute force.
item.dc:creator: Milan Rosko

item.title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
item.description: arXiv:2606.19399v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-based formal provers often collapse the verifier's output into a pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that feeds what Lean reports (error messages with their position, verified partial proofs, and remaining goals) back into proof search. Phase 1 samples N whole proofs; Phase 2 searches a tree of verified partial proofs with a Tactician, automated step repair, a Critic that ranks states and allocates the budget, and a Retriever. On miniF2F test, VERITAS solves 86.9% with Claude Haiku 5.5 and 82.8% with GPT-6 Luna, against 71.7% and 61.1% for Best-of-5 sampling, and solves more theorems than three re-implemented feedback baselines at a third to a half of their search cost. We also evaluate on 55 combinatorics problems of CombiBench and release code and run logs at https://github.com/CoderDoge1108/VERITAS.
item.dc:creator: Manish Acharya, Zhenyu Liao, Yueke Zhang, Kevin Leach, Yu Huang, Yifan Zhang

item.title: Fuss-free cumulative universes: theory and practice
item.description: arXiv:2607.11329v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Universes are central to dependent type theory, and they are notoriously difficult to handle in a way that is both correct and usable. We propose a new "fuss-free" generalised algebraic presentation for polymorphic cumulative universes that dispenses with the intricate theory of coherent universe coercions in favour of a simpler formulation, which we prove equivalent by means of a normalisation theorem for the former. We study the fuss-free formulation by means of (1) an abstract specification of its bidirectional elaboration algorithm, and (2) a concrete implementation in Haskell. We also describe and implement an extension of the fuss-free universe hierarchy with a judgemental notion of datatype description from which prior notions of cumulative inductive type may be derived.
item.dc:creator: Rapha\"el Sterbac, Jonathan Sterling

item.title: SaltBench: A Referee-Gated Protocol for Measuring Method Effects in Machine-Checked Software Work
item.description: arXiv:2609.11076v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: SaltBench asks how a machine referee changes how a coding agent works. Outcomes are decided outside the agent's toolchain; on the Claude lane a wall probed before any scored run isolates the agent from the network, reference solutions and harness, and 5 Gemini-lane cells served web search results are declared and leave every comparison; a dated freeze of predictions authorizes each run; a budget stop is a halt, never a failure. Five Rust systems components on a pinned Verus toolchain are each refereed by a withheld test suite. The arms: plain; salt-diet, also instructed to specify and verify its code (a registered reduced rendering of the method); and two arms handed the specification a priori, where the registered sign test at k=4 reached no verdict (3 of 4, p = 0.3125). salt-diet cost more on all five components, by a practical margin: no premium exceeded 2.8879x under either reading of the declared set and the three cheapest sat below 1.4x, a bound of this population and not a promise about larger ones: the premium is near 1 on the smallest components and rises with size. Versions 2 and 3 add the complete pilot matrix: 200 conditions over four models, 181 with a result of record, 16 inexpressible and 3 declared unreached at the cost cap, with no verdict on the arms. Version 3 adds a correctness reading, declared post hoc and registered after every verdict it reads existed and many had been read by its author: 447 cells pass the withheld suite, 40 fail, 10 are censored at a registered budget, 4 are unscorable and 42 are read by condition. salt-diet's pass-rate interval lies wholly below plain's on 8 greenfield and 5 brownfield rows and wholly above it on 2 greenfield rows. It is descriptive, over three cells of record per condition, with no test, and says nothing about whether the method makes code more or less correct. The full record is public.
item.dc:creator: Jason Hickey

item.title: VERDICT: Multi-Agent Parallel Modular Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.29147v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deductive verification scales to large software systems through modular reasoning, where formal contracts summarize the behavior of individual functions and enable their independent verification. Its central bottleneck is specification synthesis: constructing the contracts required for modular verification. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated specification synthesis at unprecedented scale. However, existing approaches remain fundamentally bottom-up, requiring callees to be verified before their callers. This dependency limits parallelism and provides no principled mechanism for resolving interprocedural inconsistencies that propagate across call chains. We present VERDICT, a multi-agent framework for parallelizing modular deductive verification of large-scale programs. VERDICT is built on two key principles. First, assumption-based parallel specification synthesis assigns an agent to each function and allows it to proceed immediately using assumed contracts for its callees, enabling verification to proceed in parallel across the program. Second, bidirectional interprocedural conflict reconciliation resolves the inconsistencies introduced by these assumptions: when a synthesized contract contradicts an assumption, agents propagate the necessary revisions both up and down the call graph until the contracts converge. Experimental results on real-world C programs show that VERDICT synthesizes higher-quality specifications than existing approaches while substantially reducing verification time. In particular, VERDICT is the first approach that scales to the complete 20,000-line X.509 parser, ruling out nearly all the potential runtime errors within hours, whereas prior tools like PREGUSS fall far short even after days of execution.
item.dc:creator: Tengjie Lin, Zhongyi Wang, Haokun Li, Jianwei Yin, Mingshuai Chen

item.title: What Can Postselection on Halting Decide?
item.description: arXiv:2611.20517v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A probabilistic program can produce an answer on some runs and continue forever on others. Suppose it halts with positive probability on every input and we count only the runs that halt. Aaronson et al. showed that if the correct answer must be more than twice as likely as the wrong one, such programs decide exactly the problems solvable with a finite list of halting questions chosen in advance. They asked what happens when the correct answer need only be more likely than the wrong one. We prove that the resulting class is exactly $\boldsymbol{\Delta^0_2}$: the halting questions can now be asked one at a time, with each answer helping to determine the next question. This remains true if the program must halt with probability at least 99%, or with any other prescribed rational lower bound below one. Our main technical result is the exact query bound when the program gives two guarantees. Suppose it halts with probability at least $\rho$ and, among the runs that halt, the correct answer has probability at least $a$. For rational $0 < \rho < 1$ and $1/2 < a < 1$, these programs decide exactly the problems solvable with at most $n$ halting questions chosen in advance, where $n$ is the largest integer satisfying $\rho(a/(1-a))^n \le 1$. Every value of $n$ occurs, and different values give different classes. The proof measures how much additional halting probability a change of answer requires, and counts these changes as in Ershov's hierarchy. The results extend to quantum machines with computable gates.
item.dc:creator: Saman Farhat, Farzad Didehvar

item.title: SLICR: Strategy Logic-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.27865v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. This paper introduces SLICR, a significant paradigm shift that advances the state of the art to specification-guided RL in adversarial settings under partial observability. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents' strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents' objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. We evaluate SLICR on three popular benchmarks: Predator-Prey, Google Research Football, and our home-grown extension of SMAC-HARD, demonstrating its effectiveness, scalability, and ability to adapt to diverse adversarial strategies.
item.dc:creator: Arshia Rafieioskouei, Matthew Lucas, Tzu-Han Hsu, Borzoo Bonakdarpour
